NFS2ROOT (CVE-2026-99362): pre-auth remote root in the Linux NFS server. Fixed in Debian trixie, Ubuntu still vulnerable. How to check your boxes  If any of your servers or your NAS share folders over NFS, this one is worth five minutes today.  CVE-2026-99362, named NFS2ROOT by the researchers at OpenSec, is a flaw in the Linux kernel's NFS server (nfsd). Per their write-up it goes back to Linux 3.16 and affects hosts that export NFSv4.1 or 4.2 with tcp/2049 reachable. Red Hat rates it Critical: an unauthenticated remote attacker can corrupt kernel memory, which means root with no login. OpenSec says it is keeping its exploit private, and nobody reports it being exploited yet.  Where the fixes are, as of today:  - Upstream: 6.12.117, 6.18.61, 7.3.2 and 7.4-rc1 (per OpenSec) - Debian trixie: fixed from 6.12.117. Bookworm's default 6.1 kernel is still vulnerable, but bookworm's 6.12 kernel is fixed. - Ubuntu: rated Critical (CVSS 9.8), and every supported release still shows "Vulnerable". No USN yet. - Red Hat: Critical, no fix listed yet. Default RHEL doesn't run nfsd at all.  So on Ubuntu, apt upgrade won't help yet. First check whether you're exposed at all:      systemctl is-active nfs-server     sudo exportfs -v     cat /proc/fs/nfsd/versions  If nfs-server isn't active and nothing is exported, this one doesn't affect that box. If the versions file shows +4.1 or +4.2, read on.  If you don't need NFS on that machine, turn it off:      sudo systemctl disable --now nfs-server  If you do need it, make sure 2049 only answers your own clients. With ufw, for example:      sudo ufw allow from 192.168.1.0/24 to any port 2049 proto tcp     sudo ufw deny 2049/tcp  (Change the subnet to your LAN, and check the rule order with sudo ufw status numbered.) This is also Red Hat's mitigation: disable the NFS server if you don't need it, or restrict port 2049 to trusted networks.  Question for the NAS crowd: has anyone seen a statement from TrueNAS SCALE, OpenMediaVault, Unraid or Synology about this? They all run Linux-based NFS servers, and I haven't found anything from them yet.  Sources: - Ubuntu: ubuntu.com/security/CVE-2026… - Debian tracker: security-tracker.debian.org/… - Red Hat: access.redhat.com/security/c… - OpenSec write-up: opensec.in/blog/nfs2root-cve…

Your magic link gets clicked before your user ever sees it.  Corporate mail gateways open every link in an incoming email to check it for malware. If your link spends its token on a GET, the scanner signs in and the real person gets "Link expired". They ask for a new one, the scanner eats that one too, and they give up.  The tell is in your logs: Gmail users are fine, and everyone on a company or school domain fails.  Let the link open a page and let a button do the signing in:  GET  /auth/confirm?token=...  renders a Sign in button, changes nothing POST /auth/confirm            spends the token  A scanner reads pages, but it doesn't press buttons.  How to steal it: 1. Make every GET and HEAD on auth and confirm links side-effect free. 2. Put a 6-digit code in the same email as the fallback, since scanners can't type. 3. Don't raise the expiry, the scanner gets there seconds after delivery anyway.  Which of your emails has a link that spends a token on GET?
